title: Remember me (Luke 23:32–43)
hook: a dying thief asks to be remembered and is promised paradise today

segments.voice: Yesterday, before Pilate: are you a king, and the washed hands. Your line was what is truth. Did you stay with a hard question a minute longer? Day sixty-four. A new week: the cross and the morning.

A hill outside the city walls, called the place of the skull. Calvary, in the old Latin. Three crosses. Jesus in the middle, and two criminals, one on each side. The crowd watches. Soldiers cast lots for his clothes. And the first thing Luke has Jesus say from the cross, in the Douay-Rheims, is this: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." Then the men beside him start talking. One of them joins the mocking: if you're the Christ, save yourself, and us. And the other one, who has nothing left, no time, no chance to make anything right, turns his head and says something nobody expects. Today: what he says, and what he hears back.
screen: `THE PLACE OF THE SKULL.` → `FATHER, FORGIVE THEM.` → `TWO MEN, TWO VERY DIFFERENT WORDS.`

segments.voice: The second man tells the first to stop. We deserve this, he says, but this man has done nothing wrong. Then he says to Jesus: "Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom." That's all. No speech. No list of what he did. Just remember me. And Jesus answers: "Amen I say to thee, this day thou shalt be with me in paradise." Paradise is a Persian word that came into Greek. It first meant a walled garden, the kind a king kept. Jewish writers used it for the garden of Eden, and then for the place where God keeps the righteous. So a man dying on a cross is promised a garden, and not someday. This day. Luke never gives his name. Later Christian writings call him Dismas, and Catholics know him as the good thief, honored as a saint; some ask his prayers for the dying and for prisoners. Look at what the text leaves out. No baptism is mentioned. There's no time for him to make amends, no list of sins, no promise to do better. He has one honest sentence, at the very end. The Church reads this story as a sign that mercy can reach anyone, right up to the last breath. Notice, too, what he calls the man dying next to him: Lord. And what he asks for: not to be taken down from the cross, only to be remembered.
screen: `LORD, REMEMBER ME.` · `PARADISE: A WALLED GARDEN.` · `THE GOOD THIEF, DISMAS.` · `ONE HONEST SENTENCE AT THE END.` · then, large: `THIS DAY THOU SHALT BE WITH ME IN PARADISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask to be remembered, simply. Settle and breathe. No long list, no explaining yourself. Just notice what it's like to want to be remembered, by someone you love, or by God. Let the wanting be there without dressing it up. If you pray, you can use the thief's own words, slowly, a few times: Lord, remember me. If you don't, you can just hold the wish quietly and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Remember me. What a dying thief asked for, with nothing to offer, and the answer he got: today. Today's word.
Your line: this day in paradise. Today, remember someone who might feel forgotten, and tell them so, in one plain sentence. Day sixty-four.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the good thief's words in the Passion on Good Friday, and many ask Saint Dismas to pray for the dying and for people in prison.

original.note: Greek, from a Persian word for a walled garden: the king's park, then Eden, then the place of the blessed.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice last-minute rescue.
what it means: a man with nothing to offer asks only to be remembered, and mercy reaches him at the last breath.
what a scholar hears: paradeisos, a Persian walled garden, the Greek Bible's word for Eden. and the name Dismas comes from later writings, not from Luke.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Luke 23:34, 23:42 and 23:43 given from memory; confirm.
Luke 23:34a ('Father, forgive them') is missing from some early manuscripts; the script presents it as in Luke without comment.
Paradise: Old Persian (Avestan) pairidaeza, walled enclosure, via Greek paradeisos (used in the Septuagint for Eden). Confirm.
The name Dismas comes from the apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus / Acts of Pilate; the Roman Martyrology commemorates the good thief on 25 March. Confirm and whether 'a saint' is the right phrasing.
'Patron of the dying and of prisoners' is popular devotion; confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'throw dice' became 'cast lots' (Luke 23:34); cut 'the shortest conversation in the Gospels'; cut the manuscript-punctuation paragraph (manuscript claim not in the cited text) from the teach and trapdoor; 'as far as anyone knows, he was never baptized' and 'it was enough' (narrator stating doctrine) became what the text leaves out and what the Church reads in it; 'Catholics pray to him' softened to 'some ask his prayers'; 'here's why Catholics love him so much' cut. Paradise etymology (Persian walled garden, Septuagint for Eden) kept as standard lexicon; confirm.
